title: Omar Haroun — Eudia: Outcomes, the Law-Firm Arm, and the In-House Bet for 2026
author: Omar Haroun · Richard Tromans

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Haroun accepts the cluster’s outcome-led, buyer-driven proposition and materially extends it with Eudia’s concrete AI-native delivery model: lawyers and engineers provide end-to-end outcomes while the provider absorbs some AI performance risk. He also reinforces the claim that corporate buyers’ incentives favour rapid work reallocation, while acknowledging institutional constraints. His support is primarily operating experience and customer conversations rather than measured market-wide evidence.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Haroun accepts that in-house departments are stronger AI buyers and potential substitutes for some outside work, then materially develops the proposition with an integrated AI-plus-legal-services procurement model. He argues that corporate automation priorities can conflict with preserving law-firm margins, while still recognising continuing demand for high-stakes external work and the need to prove ROI.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Haroun accepts the cluster’s organisational-redesign premise and materially extends it through an in-house-centred model combining integrated enterprise data, AI and expert lawyers, with law-firm collaboration where appropriate. His emphasis on measurable buyer outcomes rather than incremental productivity reinforces the shift toward repeatable, platform-enabled delivery, while his admission that the higher-value model is only beginning to be proved aligns with the cluster’s caution about unsettled outcomes.
qs: So, we've built a data  platform, knowledge platform, and AI platform for in-house legal teams of really um skewing towards not just Fortune 500, but what we call some of the world's most important organizations, companies where uh this isn't just about some lowhanging fruit productivity gains for doing the work incrementally better.
And again, I think I think our model of getting some of the world's best lawyers combined with this platform so that you're not just accepting this is like the low value work.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Haroun accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI will reorganise legal production rather than eliminate lawyers, and materially extends it with Eudia’s client-led model: experienced lawyers paired with AI, procurement through a services structure, outcomes rather than hours as the unit of value, and scaling through buyer-directed collaboration with incumbent partners. His support is tempered by acknowledging that the model is only beginning to be proved and by relying mainly on company experience and illustrative scenarios rather than independent results.
qs: Because ultimately to really get the value out of it, you do need some combination of humans and AI.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Haroun accepts the need to redesign workflows around expert judgment rather than merely add productivity tools, and materially extends the cluster through an operating model centred on capturing CLOs’ tacit knowledge, integrating enterprise data and existing systems, and measuring business outcomes. His broader automation and ROI claims are largely vendor assertions and do not address the cluster’s verification concerns, but they do not displace its core proposition.

kp.k: In-house focus accompanies reported tenfold revenue growth
kp.d: Speaking in January 2026, Haroun reports that Eudia exceeded its original 10 million revenue projection, crossed 20 million in December, and grew approximately tenfold from a little over two million at the start of 2025; the transcript labels the metric 'AR'. He attributes growth to initially concentrating on 10 Fortune 500 customers, identifying shared needs, and effectively launching in September 2025. These are company-reported figures, not independently substantiated results in the interview.
qs: we thought we'd be at originally 10 million uh AR. We crossed 20 in December.
It turned out to be a 10x year.
we picked initially just 10 Fortune 500 customers and went really really deep to try to uncover and discover what we could uniquely provide that they were desperate for.

kp.k: Buyer interests drive a distinct legal-AI business model
kp.d: Haroun argues that in-house teams and law firms have different, sometimes opposing interests, making 'legal tech' an insufficiently coherent category. He identifies chief legal officers as Eudia's principal champions, supported by legal operations and deputy general counsels, and reports personally meeting over 350 CLOs in 18 months. He also reports CEO and CFO engagement, positioning legal transformation as a model for other knowledge-intensive corporate functions.
qs: the needs of in-house teams are not only different but often at odds with the needs of law firms.
I've personally met over 350 chief legal officers in the past 18 months
the chief legal officer is in almost every case the main champion and person who brings UDIA in
we are seeing a lot of CEO CFO level engagement as well

kp.k: Human-AI delivery shifts execution risk onto the provider
kp.d: Haroun describes an integrated data, knowledge and AI platform combined with forward-deployed engineers or lawyers. He presents reducing outside counsel expenditure by 20% and eliminating 90% of contract review as examples of outcomes Eudia can offer, rather than documented aggregate findings. The model can replace externally sourced work or deliver internal workflows end to end; when AI falls short, additional human delivery costs reduce Eudia's gross margin.

we actually have the human component whether that's a forward deployed engineer or a forward deployed lawyer.

we actually can offer in some cases a complete replacement to work that's going externally

kp.k: AI scales expert judgment while displacing commodity work
kp.d: Haroun distinguishes rare expert knowledge from commoditized knowledge, rather than treating AI as relevant only to low-value legal tasks. He argues that AI can capture how experts generate and apply knowledge, making their judgment scalable, while commodity work is more directly automated and displaced. This is his account of the technology's trajectory, not a measured comparison of performance across work categories.
qs: knowledge can be divided into knowledge that's rare and knowledge that's commoditized.
there's now this incredible opportunity to actually scale the judgment and expert knowledge with AI.
On the more commodity work, I think that's that's more just completely sort of getting automated and displaced.

kp.k: Law-firm structures ease procurement without selling hours
kp.d: Tromans frames Eudia's structure as including the acquisition of Ireland-based ALSP Johnson Hannah and an Arizona law firm operating in an alternative-business-structure jurisdiction. Haroun distinguishes engagement through the law firm from the former Johnson Hannah operation, now described as Eudia Europe. His substantive rationale is that legal departments often buy services more easily than software; the law-firm arm makes technology easier to procure while retaining output- or outcome-based units of value, rather than hours or headcount.
qs: it's actually much easier for an in-house legal team at times to engage with a law firm than it is to engage with a technology company.
for customers who engage our law firm there's an engagement letter
we would never even allow the unit of value to be the number of hours or the number of humans.
It needs to be something output or outcome based.

kp.k: Experienced lawyers underpin the higher-value delivery proposition
kp.d: Haroun says Eudia sells the combined capability of experienced lawyers and its platform, not merely a claim that its diligence software is superior. He illustrates this with a former Gibson Dunn lawyer whom customers would historically pay $1,000 an hour, and a deal historically requiring 30 such people. He claims highly trained humans in the loop improve quality and align delivery with faster client outcomes; the interview provides no controlled quality or staffing comparison.
qs: the kind of person that most of our customers would pay $1,000 an hour to to do their M&A um diligence work and historically need 30 of those people to really get a deal done.
The pitch is hey one of our M&A lawyers.
the quality is just much higher when you have the human in the loop.
get back issues lists in five minutes instead of, you know, five days

kp.k: Client-directed platform use enables cooperation with incumbent firms
kp.d: Haroun explicitly corrects the suggestion that Eudia receives revenue from law firms: firms use the platform, typically initially at corporate customers' direction, but are not paying customers. He reports unexpected receptiveness among leading firms and forward-thinking partners, particularly in M&A and litigation, and interprets this as recognition that AI changes work rather than necessarily eliminating their roles. Eudia does not insist that clients use its own law firm.
qs: we're not getting revenue from law firms, but we are having law firms use our platform and that's typically initially at the direction of the customers
We've actually been surprised how receptive at least like the top law firms and the very forward thinking individual partners have been.
AI is not actually coming for their job. It's just changing the work.

kp.k: Litigation applications extend beyond discovery into trial support
kp.d: Responding to Tromans's discovery framing, Haroun says Eudia's litigation work has predominantly involved high-stakes matters at pre-trial or trial stages. He describes using accumulated client knowledge and newly ingested data to flag inconsistencies in witness statements and improve information retrieval for litigators. Winning litigation is presented as the desired outcome, not an evidenced result of platform use.

being able to flag inconsistencies
it's not the discovery work as much as it is the um really really next level how do we think about the outcome being winning the litigation

kp.k: Integrated client data supports tentative business-outcome insights
kp.d: Haroun describes the client 'brain' as an intelligence layer and unified data platform connected to existing enterprise systems, with forward-deployed engineering central to deployment beyond pilots. He says 100 contracts plus financial and operational data can demonstrate value. In one customer example, contract language was associated with margins 50 basis points higher, but he expressly cautions that the conclusion might not hold across the full dataset. He distinguishes such analytics from expenditure reduction through taking over and automating workflows.

We could have 100 contracts along with the requisite financial and operational data
when you use this language in your contracts your margin is actually 50 basis points higher

kp.k: Principles-based judgment could replace excessive rules-based redlining
kp.d: Haroun reports a customer's view that redlining is a crutch for people who do not know how to do deals. His own argument is that senior CLOs balance speed and risk using contextual judgment, whereas playbooks passed to juniors or outsiders encourage defensive risk aversion and repeated redlining, ultimately requiring senior intervention. He proposes capturing expert principles to reduce or eliminate that process, presenting deals closing 90% faster as an intended outcome rather than an established result.
qs: he said he believes redlinining is a crutch for people who don't know how to do deals
each person in the value chain actually is now incentivized to be more riskaverse because no one gets fired by being more riskaverse.
shifting I would say the whole industry from this very kind of uh processheavy rules-based approach to a more um outcomeheavy principlesbased approach.
We're actually trying to get rid of redlinining right in some sense because that would actually then unlock the outcome of closing deals in 90% faster.

kp.k: Undocumented expertise constitutes the proposed competitive advantage
kp.d: Haroun rejects a simple claim that data alone is the competitive moat. He instead identifies experts' undocumented knowledge, acquired through close engagement with CLOs and with their consent, as the distinctive asset. His stated aim is to translate intuition into data and surface relevant information that makes expert decisions more data-driven, rather than merely digitizing existing documents.
qs: My my view is the undocumented knowledge of experts is actually the moat
with with with their consent, of course

kp.k: Incumbent incentives may slow fundamental market restructuring
kp.d: Responding to Tromans's question about AI-first firms entering the AmLaw 100, Haroun suggests a roughly three-year horizon for such change, while emphasizing entrenched institutions, incentives and lobbies. He argues that vendors serving both firms and legal departments face conflicting incentives when preserving firm margins conflicts with corporate automation goals. He also views partnership consensus and partners approaching retirement as impediments to rapid self-disruption. These are strategic judgments and forecasts, not established industry-wide findings.
qs: the next three years is where I see something like that happening
fundamental change is not that it just can't be that fast when you have these extremely entrenched institutions and incentives

They're not here to help train the lawyers in the future. They're not here to help law firms preserve their margins.

kp.k: Partner competition could exchange lower fees for greater volume
kp.d: Haroun envisages scaling through cooperating incumbent partners rather than continually hiring Eudia lawyers. His hypothetical client conducts 20 M&A deals annually and consolidates work among one or two of five existing firms whose partners accept the model. A partner might forgo 50% of revenue per deal but receive 10 deals instead of two. He predicts competition for client share, alongside adoption of client-preferred technology, could trigger broader market change; the figures illustrate a mechanism rather than report observed transactions.

even though they're foregoing 50% of the revenue they would have gotten on each deal they may now get 10 deals instead of two deals right

kp.k: Second-half 2026 scrutiny will prioritize measurable AI returns
kp.d: Haroun predicts that early-2026 enthusiasm for AI tools will give way in the second half of the year to demands for tangible ROI and business outcomes. He connects this to corporate mandates involving headcount, costs and other value measures, arguing that user satisfaction alone will not justify organization-wide licenses costing $500 per month each. He reports about a dozen customers nearing the point of sharing accounts framed around $25 million of hard value, but supplies no underlying calculations or individual case evidence.

kp.k: Avoiding feasible automation is framed as an ethical failure
kp.d: Asked whether relatively small legal budgets weaken incentives to change, Haroun argues that legal work is especially exposed to language models and reports anecdotal CEO frustration at paying firms for apparently automatable manual work. He characterizes continued payment for such work as potentially approaching a dereliction of duty and states that not using AI is unethical. Tromans introduces the explicit fiduciary-duty framing; neither speaker establishes a legal obligation, and Haroun acknowledges justified concerns about AI bias.

the very justified challenges in terms of bias

kp.k: Partnerships and specialization may replace build-everything strategies
kp.d: Haroun's second principal 2026 prediction is greater recognition that technology providers cannot build everything themselves, potentially producing consolidation, clearer areas of specialization and more partnerships. He distinguishes mature enterprise workflow capabilities from deep legal-AI expertise, and hopes contract lifecycle management and discovery providers will cooperate with AI-native companies even while developing AI of their own. This is a forecast and recommendation, not a report of completed partnerships.
qs: none of us are going to be able to build everything on our own.
whether that means more consolidation, whether that means just people being more clear about their swim lanes
we're going to start to see more partnerships with technology companies
they will have their own AI but that may not be what they're natively going to be best at

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Omar Haroun predicts a shift toward AI-enabled, outcome-based legal services that automate commodity work, scale expert judgment, and compete on demonstrable corporate value.
pts.d: Haroun distinguishes commodity knowledge work, which he says is being automated and displaced, from rare expert knowledge, which AI can scale. He presents Eudia's platform combined with deployed lawyers and engineers as a means of delivering end-to-end outcomes rather than merely selling productivity software. Examples he offers include reducing outside-counsel spending by 20% and eliminating 90% of contract review; these are stated capabilities, not independently established results. He argues that expert human involvement improves quality and that the provider can absorb AI shortcomings through lower gross margins. Eudia's law-firm arm and services operation also make procurement easier for in-house teams, while the unit of value remains outputs or outcomes rather than hours or staffing. Haroun describes an ambition to replace rules-driven redlining with principles-based application of senior judgment, potentially closing deals 90% faster. He says Eudia already supports high-stakes litigation through customer-specific knowledge, inconsistency detection, and data access, rather than primarily discovery. He predicts that client-directed platform use and competition for a larger share of client matters can induce individual law-firm partners to accept lower revenue per matter. He also predicts stronger scrutiny of AI return on investment and more partnerships, clearer specialisation, or consolidation among technology providers. His claim that not using AI can be unethical is a normative argument about avoidable manual costs, not a reported legal ruling.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Haroun principally supports his claims with Eudia's commercial experience, customer interactions, illustrative workflows, and hypothetical economics; no independent benchmark or systematic study is supplied.
pts.d: Haroun reports exceeding an original revenue projection of 10 million and crossing 20 million in December, describing 2025 as a tenfold-growth year. These commercial figures support his account of demand, rather than directly demonstrating legal-work quality or customer savings. He says Eudia initially worked deeply with ten Fortune 500 customers and that he personally met more than 350 chief legal officers over 18 months. His examples include an experienced M&A lawyer paired with the platform, customer-directed use by outside law firms, and litigation support using accumulated client knowledge. He explicitly clarifies that law firms use the platform but do not currently generate revenue for Eudia. A limited-data example links particular contract language with a 50-basis-point margin difference, but Haroun acknowledges that the finding might not hold across the full dataset. He says about a dozen customers are approaching the point of sharing substantial hard-value results, using $25 million as the figure in his description, without providing customer-level calculations. The example of a partner relinquishing 50% of revenue per deal but receiving ten deals instead of two is hypothetical, not an observed market result. His comments about CEO frustration are expressly anecdotal. His ethical position references a paper he says he wrote, without presenting its analysis.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: From the interview's January 2026 standpoint, Haroun expects ROI scrutiny in the second half of 2026 and more fundamental market change over approximately three years, subject to proof, integration, and institutional constraints.
pts.d: Haroun expects the first half of 2026 to continue the rush to acquire AI tools, followed roughly six months later by demands for tangible outcomes and ROI. He forecasts more technology partnerships during 2026, while framing collaboration among legal technology incumbents and AI-native companies partly as a hope. Responding to a discussion of AI-first providers reaching major-firm scale, he offers the next three years as his horizon for change of that kind; he does not provide a precise revenue forecast or guaranteed ranking-entry date. He stresses that entrenched institutions, incentives, and lobbies limit the speed of fundamental change. His proposed sequence is first to prove repeatedly that expert lawyers plus the platform can deliver increasingly high-value work, then to generate competitive pressure as incumbent partners adopt client-preferred technology to win more matters. Outcomes depend on relevant customer data, integration with existing systems, access to expert knowledge with consent, and skilled human participation. He says partnership governance and partners nearing retirement make rapid self-disruption difficult. His automation argument does not imply universal replacement of elite lawyers: he expects substantial continuing work in high-stakes litigation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims centre on large corporate legal buyers, their external providers, expert lawyers, and enterprise technology suppliers rather than individual access to justice.
pts.d: Eudia targets in-house teams at Fortune 500 companies and other major organisations. Haroun identifies chief legal officers as the principal champions, with legal operations leaders and deputy general counsel involved in deployment, and growing CEO/CFO attention to enterprise outcomes. These buyers face pressure to demonstrate savings, business value, and sometimes headcount-related results. Commodity legal work performed internally or externally is the principal displacement category; he does not quantify job losses. Senior experts are positioned as sources of scalable judgment, while individual outside-firm partners may preserve or expand total business through lower per-matter revenue and greater matter volume. Traditional partnerships face decision-making barriers, and vendors serving both firms and in-house teams face what Haroun characterises as conflicting incentives between preserving provider margins and automating buyer costs. Eudia's law-firm and ALSP services components deliver work, whereas software vendors supply technology; Haroun's model combines these functions without treating them as identical. CLM, e-discovery, and broader enterprise platform suppliers are potential integration partners. The corporate savings discussed are not claims about closing the civil justice gap.
